799.title: The Peace of God
799.hook: church councils try to protect peasants, pilgrims and clergy from knights' violence
799.howItsDone: Catholics remember the Peace and Truce of God as an early attempt by the Church to limit violence; today the Church keeps a World Day of Peace each New Year's Day, and parishes pray for peace in the prayers of the faithful.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cluny: a duke who signed away every claim on a monastery. Your line was free to pray. Did your slice of quiet survive the day? Today, the Church tries to make peace without an army. Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

The saints have been carried out of their churches. Their relics, in boxes of wood and silver, sit in an open field, and a crowd has walked in from the villages to stand around them: farmers, monks, mothers with children on their hips. Bishops are there too. And so are knights, the men with the horses and the swords, the men who, in this time and place, nobody can easily stop. The bishops ask them to put their hands on the relics and swear. Swear to what? That's today's word: the Peace of God.
screen: `RELICS IN AN OPEN FIELD.` → `A CROWD AND THE KNIGHTS.` → `PUT YOUR HAND ON THE SAINTS AND SWEAR.`

segments.voice: Start with the trouble. In parts of France, there was often no king strong enough to keep order. Local lords and their armed men settled quarrels by raiding, and the ones who suffered were the ones without weapons: peasants, travelers, clergy. Next, the Peace. Church councils met and named the people who were off limits. The canons of one such council, at Charroux, are blunt. Anyone who breaks into a church and robs it, anyone who steals a poor farmer's animals, anyone who strikes a cleric who carries no weapons, is cut off from the Church until he makes amends. Later councils widened the circle of the protected. Then, the Truce. A second idea grew beside the first. If the fighting couldn't be ended, maybe it could be paused. The Truce of God named days of the week and holy seasons, like Advent and Lent, when no one was to fight at all. The rules differed from council to council, but the shape was the same: some time belongs to God, and no sword may cross it. Finally, why it matters. The bishops had no army. What they had was the faith of the crowd, the saints, and Jesus's words, which in the Douay-Rheims read: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." The Peace and the Truce didn't end the violence, and oaths were broken. But they drew a line around the weak and said out loud that even a knight answers for whom he hurts. That's today's line: truce of god.
screen: `NO KING, AND KNIGHTS UNCHECKED.` · `THE PEACE: HANDS OFF THE DEFENSELESS.` · `THE TRUCE: DAYS WITHOUT FIGHTING.` · `A LINE AROUND THE WEAK.` · then, large: `TRUCE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: protect someone weaker. For the sit, let one person come to mind who has less power than others around them. A new coworker. A child. An older neighbor. The one in the group chat everybody talks over. Hold them in mind without fixing anything yet. Then ask: where could I stand between them and some small harm today? An interruption I could stop. A joke I could refuse to laugh at. If you pray, you can hold them before God with the line, blessed are the peacemakers. The bell holds the time.
The Peace of God. Church councils naming the defenseless, peasants, clergy, travelers, and calling armed men to swear to leave them be. Today's word.
Your line: truce of god. Today, call a small truce of your own: one hour, one conversation, where you won't strike back. Keep it, even if no one notices. Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

800.title: Anselm (1033–1109)
800.hook: faith seeking understanding, and God as that than which nothing greater can be thought
800.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Anselm as a Doctor of the Church, and his motto, faith seeking understanding, is often used to describe the work of theology; students still read his Proslogion in philosophy and theology classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Peace of God: councils drawing a line around the defenseless. Your line was truce of god. Did you keep your small truce? Today, a monk who thinks his way toward God. Day eight hundred.

A monk at the abbey of Bec has already written one book about God, a long chain of arguments. Now he wants something shorter: one single argument that needs nothing else to stand on. He hunts for it, and it slips away. He decides the hunt is a distraction and tries to stop, and the thought won't leave him alone. Then, he says, it came. He wrote it up as a prayer, and he tested it against a line monks sang in choir, in the Douay-Rheims: "The fool hath said in his heart: There is no God." Today's word is the monk: Anselm.
screen: `ONE ARGUMENT, NOTHING ELSE NEEDED.` → `IT WOULDN'T LEAVE HIM ALONE.` → `THE FOOL HATH SAID IN HIS HEART.`

segments.voice: Start with the motto. In the preface to the book, the Proslogion, Anselm says he first gave it the title faith seeking understanding. The order matters. In the opening chapter he says, in effect: I don't seek to understand so that I may believe; I believe so that I may understand. Faith is where he starts. Then it goes looking. Next, the name. Anselm offers one for God: that than which nothing greater can be thought. Then he turns to the fool. When the fool hears those words, he understands them, so the idea is at least in his mind. But, Anselm reasons, if it were only in the mind, you could think of something greater: the same thing, existing in reality too. So it must exist in both. Then, the answer. A monk named Gaunilo wrote back on the fool's behalf. By that logic, he said, I could prove a perfect island exists just by picturing one. Anselm wrote a reply, and the objection and the reply are still read with the book. Catholic thinkers have weighed the argument differently; Thomas Aquinas, later, did not accept it as a proof. Finally, the surprise. A few chapters on, Anselm goes further. God, he says, is not only that than which nothing greater can be thought, but something greater than can be thought at all. The book that reaches toward God with careful logic arrives at the edge of the mind and says so. For Anselm, that wasn't defeat. It was the point. That's today's line: faith seeking understanding.
screen: `I BELIEVE SO THAT I MAY UNDERSTAND.` · `NOTHING GREATER CAN BE THOUGHT.` · `GAUNILO AND THE PERFECT ISLAND.` · `GREATER THAN CAN BE THOUGHT.` · then, large: `FAITH SEEKING UNDERSTANDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about God, on purpose, for the length of the sit. Not to win an argument. Take Anselm's phrase and turn it slowly: that than which nothing greater can be thought. Try to think of something greater. Notice where your mind runs out. If you pray, let the thinking turn into prayer whenever it wants to, the way Anselm's book does. If you don't, treat it as a puzzle worth two minutes of your attention. If you'd like a third minute, keep going after the bell. The bell holds the time.
Anselm. A monk and teacher who called his book faith seeking understanding, and named God that than which nothing greater can be thought. Today's word.
Your line: faith seeking understanding. Today, take one thing you hold to be true and ask it one honest question. Let the question walk with you. Day eight hundred.

801.title: Cîteaux (1098)
801.hook: monks seek a simpler, stricter Benedictine life in white habits
801.howItsDone: Cistercian monks and nuns, including the Trappists, still live by the Rule of Saint Benedict with manual work, silence and the hours of prayer, and their abbey churches are kept plain; some abbeys welcome guests for retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anselm, the monk who called his book faith seeking understanding. What honest question did you ask? Today, monks who decided they wanted less. Day eight hundred one.

An iron candlestick. A cross of painted wood, not gold. Walls of bare stone, and light coming in through plain glass. Stand in an old Cistercian church and the first thing you may notice is what isn't there. No crowd of carved monsters on the columns. No silver on the altar. Just stone, light, and the sound of a few voices singing psalms. The builders chose less, on purpose. Today's word is the name of the monks who chose it: Cistercian.
screen: `AN IRON CANDLESTICK.` → `WHAT ISN'T THERE.` → `LESS, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Start with the leaving. Robert, abbot of a monastery called Molesme, came to think that he and his monks weren't keeping the Rule of Saint Benedict as it was written. So he left, with a group of brothers, and founded what the early accounts simply call the New Monastery, in a wild, lonely place called Cîteaux. Next, what they cut. Their own early account says they set aside whatever they couldn't find in the Rule: fur garments, undershirts, extra dishes at table. They went back to working the land with their own hands. They wore habits of undyed wool, which is why people came to call them the white monks. Then, the churches. Early Cistercian rules ask for crosses of painted wood, not gold or silver, and candlesticks of iron. The aim wasn't ugliness. It was attention: nothing in the room competing with prayer. Finally, the bond. One of the early abbots, Stephen Harding, is credited with a Charter of Charity linking the new houses, so they kept one way of life and looked after one another. Cluny and Cîteaux both followed Benedict, and the Church honors saints from each; they heard the same Rule in different keys. Jesus says to Martha, in the Douay-Rheims: "thou art careful, and art troubled about many things: But one thing is necessary." Some readers hear the whole Cistercian plan in that sentence. That's today's line: plainer.
screen: `LEAVING FOR THE NEW MONASTERY.` · `CUT WHAT ISN'T IN THE RULE.` · `PAINTED WOOD, IRON, PLAIN GLASS.` · `A CHARTER OF CHARITY.` · then, large: `PLAINER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: simplify one thing. For the sit, look around the room you're in, or walk through your day in your mind. Find one thing that crowds out what matters: a cluttered corner, an app you open without meaning to, a commitment you keep out of habit. Don't fix it yet. Just see it plainly, and let yourself feel the space it would leave. If you pray, you can rest in Jesus's words to Martha: one thing is necessary. After the bell, take one small step: clear the corner, move the app, let one thing go. The bell holds the time.
Cistercian. A monk or nun of the way of life born at Cîteaux: the Rule of Benedict kept closely, in undyed wool, with plain churches and work of the hands. Today's word.
Your line: plainer. Today, when you're about to add one more thing, pause and ask whether one less would do. Then choose. Day eight hundred one.

802.title: Bernard on love
802.hook: we love ourselves, then God for ourselves, then God for God, and at last ourselves for God
802.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Bernard of Clairvaux as a Doctor of the Church; his On Loving God and his sermons on the Song of Songs are read in monasteries and by people making retreats, and his feast is kept in late summer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Cistercians, the white monks of Cîteaux. Your line was plainer. What did you let go of? Today, a Cistercian abbot writes about love. Day eight hundred two.

A small girl visits her grandmother because there are cookies. That's the honest truth of it. Years later, she still visits, but now it's for the grandmother: the stories, the laugh, the hands. Later still, long after the cookies stopped mattering, she notices something odd. The person she has become was shaped by those visits. Loving her grandmother changed how she loves herself. A monk wrote a whole ladder of love along those lines, except the one he was climbing toward was God. Today's word is his name and his subject: Bernard on love.
screen: `FIRST, THE COOKIES.` → `THEN, THE GRANDMOTHER.` → `A LADDER OF LOVE.`

segments.voice: Start with the question. Bernard was a Cistercian abbot at a monastery called Clairvaux. Someone asked him why God should be loved, and how much. His answer opens his little book On Loving God: the reason for loving God is God, and the measure is to love without measure. Then he sets out a ladder. Next, the first two rungs. At first, Bernard says, we love ourselves, for our own sake. That's where people begin, and he doesn't scold it. Then trouble comes, and we turn to God for help. Now we love God, but still for our own sake, for what God gives. Bernard counts that as real love, a true step up. Then, the third rung. Keep coming back for help, he says, and something shifts. You begin to taste how good God is, and you love God not for what you get but because God is good. In the Douay-Rheims, the first letter of John puts the root of it plainly: "Let us therefore love God, because God first hath loved us." Finally, the top rung, the strangest. You love even yourself only for God's sake. Bernard isn't sure anyone fully reaches it in this life; he wonders aloud whether it waits for the next. Elsewhere, preaching on the Song of Songs, he says love needs no reward beyond itself: I love because I love. The ladder starts with need and ends there, with love that asks for nothing back. That's today's line: love for love's sake.
screen: `LOVE WITHOUT MEASURE.` · `FIRST FOR OURSELVES.` · `THEN GOD, FOR GOD'S SAKE.` · `AT LAST, OURSELVES FOR GOD.` · then, large: `LOVE FOR LOVE'S SAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love one thing for its own sake. For the sit, choose one thing you love: a person, a place, a piece of music, the light in a certain window. Hold it in mind. Notice how much of the love is about what it gives you. That's all right; Bernard starts there too. Then try, just for a moment, to love it simply because it's good. Not useful. Good. If you pray, you can let that turn toward God, who, the letter of John says, loved first. The bell holds the time.
Bernard on love. A Cistercian abbot's ladder: from loving ourselves, to loving God for what God gives, to loving God for God's sake, and at last ourselves for God. Today's word.
Your line: love for love's sake. Today, do one kind thing for someone that can't possibly come back to you. Don't mention it. Day eight hundred two.

803.title: Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179)
803.hook: abbess, composer, healer and visionary, named a Doctor of the Church
803.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Hildegard as a Doctor of the Church; her chants are sung by choirs and recorded, her writings are read on retreat, and the community at Eibingen keeps her memory by the Rhine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernard on love, a ladder from loving ourselves to loving God for God's sake. Your line was love for love's sake. Today, a nun who once wrote to Bernard himself, asking his counsel about what she saw. Day eight hundred three.

A sung play. On stage, a soul, a chorus of virtues, and the devil. Everyone sings except the devil. He only shouts. The woman who wrote it also wrote songs for her sisters to sing in chapel, books on plants and healing, and letters that told popes and emperors exactly what she thought. She led a community of nuns by the river Rhine, and she said she saw visions. Today's word is her name: Hildegard of Bingen.
screen: `EVERYONE SINGS BUT THE DEVIL.` → `SONGS, PLANTS, LETTERS.` → `A NUN BY THE RHINE.`

segments.voice: Start with the visions. Hildegard was a Benedictine nun, and later an abbess. She says she saw visions from childhood and kept quiet about them for a long time. Then, at the opening of her book Scivias, she writes that a fiery light poured into her mind, and a voice told her to write what she saw and heard. Doubt held her back, she says, until illness pressed her, and she began, with help from a monk and one of her sisters. The book's title means, roughly, know the ways. Next, the music. Hildegard wrote chants for the liturgy, long, soaring lines for her community to sing, and that play of the virtues, where the soul is pulled between them and the devil who cannot sing. Then, the green. A word runs through her writing: viriditas, greenness. For her it meant the life God pours into everything: sap in a branch, health in a body, freshness in a soul. A soul could dry up. It could also turn green again. It's the psalm's picture, in the Douay-Rheims: a person who is "like a tree which is planted near the running waters". Finally, the range. She wrote about herbs and healing, preached, and wrote letters to the powerful without softening her words. Centuries after her death, Pope Benedict the Sixteenth named her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Church. Visionary, composer, healer, abbess, and in all of it, the same conviction: life is given, and a dried-up soul can turn green again. That's today's line: the green life.
screen: `WRITE WHAT YOU SEE AND HEAR.` · `CHANTS AND A PLAY OF VIRTUES.` · `VIRIDITAS: GREENNESS.` · `A DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.` · then, large: `THE GREEN LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, in two parts. Now, for the sit: notice something green, a plant on the sill, a tree outside, moss on a wall, or one you remember. Look at it the way Hildegard might: life, given, not made by you. Breathe with it. If you pray, you can hold the psalm's picture, a tree planted near the running waters. Later today, look up a recording of one of Hildegard's chants and listen to one all the way through, with nothing else going on. The bell holds the time.
Hildegard of Bingen. A Benedictine abbess, visionary, composer and healer, who spoke of viriditas, the green life God gives, and was named a Doctor of the Church. Today's word.
Your line: the green life. Today, water something, a plant, a friendship, a project gone dry, and give it one small drink of attention. Day eight hundred three.

804.title: The Crusades, honestly
804.hook: armed pilgrimages that included massacres in Jerusalem and attacks on Jewish communities
804.howItsDone: Catholics pray for peace in the Holy Land at Mass and in parish intentions, and the Church's own acts of repentance, like the Day of Pardon in the jubilee year, name the violence of the past alongside its faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hildegard of Bingen and viriditas, the life God gives. Your line was the green life. What did you water? Today's story is harder, and it asks for honesty. Day eight hundred four.

A piece of cloth, cut in the shape of a cross, sewn onto a tunic at the shoulder. In the accounts of that day, a pope has just finished preaching to a crowd in France, and people are pressing forward to vow that they'll go east. Farmers, knights, priests. Some will walk all the way to Jerusalem. They think of themselves as pilgrims. They are also an army. Today's word holds both of those at once, and today's line asks us not to drop either half. The word is crusade.
screen: `A CLOTH CROSS AT THE SHOULDER.` → `PILGRIMS, AND AN ARMY.` → `HOLD BOTH HALVES.`

segments.voice: Start with the call. Pope Urban the Second urged Western Christians to go east, to help Christians there and to reach Jerusalem. The accounts that survive disagree about his exact words. Those who answered took a vow and marked themselves with the cross. So a crusade was an armed pilgrimage: prayer and penance, joined to war. Next, what happened before they even left Europe. Bands of crusaders turned on Jewish communities in towns along the Rhine. Jewish chronicles from those towns remember the dead, and families who chose death over forced baptism. Some bishops sheltered Jewish families; some could not stop the killing. Then, Jerusalem. When the crusaders took the city, they killed its people, Muslims and Jews, in the streets and in holy places. A Christian chronicler who was there describes the slaughter without shame. Finally, telling it honestly. Even then, there were voices from inside the Church. When a monk later stirred up attacks on Jews during another crusade, Bernard of Clairvaux wrote that the Jews were not to be persecuted, and went in person to silence him. And in a jubilee year, Pope John Paul the Second led the Church in asking God's forgiveness for violence used in the service of the truth, and for sins against the people of Israel. Telling it honestly means keeping both halves: the faith that made people walk so far, and the crimes some of them committed on the way. That's today's line: tell it honestly.
screen: `AN ARMED PILGRIMAGE.` · `ATTACKS ALONG THE RHINE.` · `SLAUGHTER IN JERUSALEM.` · `VOICES OF SORROW AND PARDON.` · then, large: `TELL IT HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray, or hope, for peace in the Holy Land. For the sit, hold the land in mind, its hills and old stone streets, and the people who live there now, of every faith, and those who are grieving there today. Don't take a side in your head. Just hold them. If you pray, the Douay-Rheims psalm gives you the words: pray ye for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem. If you don't pray, hold them with a wish for their safety. The bell holds the time.
Crusade. An armed pilgrimage under the sign of the cross, joining prayer and penance to war, and carrying both faith and grave crimes. Today's word.
Your line: tell it honestly. Today, when you tell a story about your own side, your family, your team, your town, include the part that doesn't flatter you. Day eight hundred four.

805.title: Francis and the sultan (1219)
805.hook: in the middle of a crusade Francis crosses the lines to talk with Sultan al-Kamil
805.howItsDone: Franciscans remember the meeting at Damietta as part of their calling, and Catholic and Muslim groups sometimes recall it when they meet for dialogue; Franciscan friars still serve at holy sites in the Holy Land.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Crusades, told honestly. Your line was tell it honestly. This week ran from the Peace of God, through Anselm, the Cistercians, Bernard and Hildegard, to that hard story. Today, one man walks out of it. Day eight hundred five.

Outside the Egyptian city of Damietta, two armies face each other. A crusader army, camped and waiting. The sultan's army, across the way. Between them is ground nobody crosses unless they mean to fight. A man in a rough habit walks out into it anyway, with one companion and no weapon. He isn't carrying a message from the generals. He wants to talk to the sultan himself. Today's word is that meeting: Francis and the sultan.
screen: `TWO ARMIES AT DAMIETTA.` → `GROUND NOBODY CROSSES.` → `A MAN IN A ROUGH HABIT.`

segments.voice: Start with the crossing. A bishop in the crusader camp, Jacques de Vitry, wrote about it. Francis, he says, went over to the sultan's side unarmed. Soldiers seized him on the road, and he told them he was a Christian and asked to be taken to their lord. Next, the welcome. The sultan, al-Kamil, received him. Jacques writes that the sultan listened to Francis preach for some days, then had him taken back safely to the Christian camp, and asked him to pray for him. Then, the stories that grew. A later life of Francis, by Bonaventure, adds more: that Francis offered to walk through fire to show his faith, and the sultan declined; that the sultan offered him rich gifts, and Francis refused them. These come later, and some readers take them as legend. What the eyewitness gives is simpler: two men on opposite sides of a war, and a conversation. Finally, what Francis carried home. In a rule he wrote for his brothers, he tells those who go among Muslims there are two ways to live. One is to preach, when they see it pleases God. The other, which he puts first, is not to argue or quarrel, but to be subject to every human creature for God's sake. That's a line from the first letter of Peter, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be ye subject therefore to every human creature for God's sake." Francis didn't end the war. He walked through it, and his rule gives his brothers a way of living beside people who are not like them. That's today's line: across the lines.
screen: `UNARMED INTO THE SULTAN'S CAMP.` · `THE SULTAN HEARS HIM.` · `LATER STORIES OF FIRE AND GIFTS.` · `FIRST, DO NOT QUARREL.` · then, large: `ACROSS THE LINES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: talk with someone on the other side. For the sit, bring to mind one person across a line from you: politics, a family quarrel, a rival team, a different faith. Hold their face, not their side. Ask yourself what you'd want to know if you only wanted to understand them. Find one question. If you pray, you can hold them before God for a breath or two. Then decide when, this week, you'll ask it, and listen to the answer without arguing back. The bell holds the time.
Francis and the sultan. In the middle of a crusade, Francis of Assisi crossed the lines unarmed, and Sultan al-Kamil received him and heard him out. Today's word.
Your line: across the lines. Today, cross one small line: sit with someone you usually avoid, or ask someone you disagree with how they came to see it that way. Day eight hundred five.

fork.setup: you're Francis, in a crusader camp outside a besieged city. the armies are dug in. what do you do?
options: take up a sword with the others.
cross to the sultan's camp, unarmed, and ask to speak with him.
go home to Assisi.
fork.reveal: Francis crossed unarmed, told the soldiers who seized him that he was a Christian, and asked to see their lord. al-Kamil received him.

trapdoor: what you thought: Francis and the sultan is a gentle story about getting along.
what it means: in the middle of a war, Francis crossed the lines unarmed, and Sultan al-Kamil received him and heard him.
what a scholar hears: an eyewitness bishop's account, later details in Bonaventure, and a rule telling brothers first not to quarrel.
